claims.text: The target material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
The elevated-temperature performance of the unmodified titanium–nickel-based alloy has not been established.
The intervention adds 0.5–1.0 wt.% Y2O3 during mechanical alloying and consolidation.
Mechanical alloying followed by consolidation such as spark plasma sintering will produce a uniform dispersion of fine Y2O3 particles.
The intervention will produce fine, stable Y2O3 nanoparticles embedded in the alloy matrix.
Nanoscale second-phase particles can contribute to high-temperature strengthening in a high-entropy alloy.
Y2O3 particles will pin grain boundaries and inhibit grain-boundary migration at elevated temperature.
Y2O3 particles will hinder dislocation motion through oxide-dispersion strengthening.
The oxide dispersion will reduce thermal coarsening of the alloy microstructure.
The oxide dispersion will reduce dynamic recovery and grain growth during high-temperature exposure.
Adding Y2O3 will increase elevated-temperature yield strength relative to an identically processed alloy without Y2O3.
Adding Y2O3 will improve creep resistance relative to an identically processed alloy without Y2O3.
The proposed intervention is applicable to single-phase HEAs in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
The relevant elevated-temperature test range is approximately 600–1000 °C.
The intervention may be useful in extreme environments requiring oxidation resistance.
Thermal aging can soften a titanium-containing refractory HEA through impurity-promoted phase segregation and depletion of strengthening interstitials.
The optimal Y2O3 concentration and its interactions with the base-alloy elements are uncertain.
It is uncertain whether processing will reproducibly achieve a nanoparticle distribution that stabilizes the microstructure throughout the target temperature range.
